title: Rejuvenating the Ecological Self: Traditional Indian Theories as Interpretative Frameworks for Environmental Well-Being
abstract: Conventional psychological models often frame well-being as a private, internal state, frequently neglecting the active role of cultural and material environments. This article proposes a philosophy-driven psycho-cultural account of well-being by analysing Indian sculpture and architecture as indigenous psychological systems. Drawing on Rasa theory, Ayurvedic ecology, and the Bhāva–Rasa framework, the study argues that well-being is an emergent property of embodied engagement with culturally meaningful spaces. By mapping these indigenous frameworks onto constructs such as the dialogical self and semiotic mediation, the paper demonstrates how traditional built environments function as active modulators of affective grammar. The analysis moves beyond “restoration” (the recovery from cognitive depletion) to “instoration” (the active cultivation of personal and ethical competencies), positioning the Indian aesthetical tradition as a tool for psychological rejuvenation. Through a synthesis of the Rasa framework and contemporary environmental psychology, the article calls for a shift toward an “ecological mind.” It concludes by proposing a research agenda that integrates biometric tools, such as eye-tracking, to measure how traditional semiotic nodes foster cognitive recovery and emotional equilibrium in the modern built environment.
